implementation_notes: In C++ the transport is a library concern and only the check registry is left to write: with the header-only cpp-httplib the endpoint is svr.Get("/healthz", handler) on an httplib::Server whose handler sets httplib::Response::status and the body (Boost.Beast or Drogon occupy the same role where a full async HTTP framework is already in the stack). What replaces the classic structure is therefore the route registration plus a registry object the handler consults with a per-check deadline; the classic form is still justified for the aggregation policy - which checks count for liveness, which for readiness, and how their statuses combine. Note that cpp-httplib is blocking and HTTP/1.1-only, so a health route served from the same thread pool as traffic can be starved by slow requests: a separate server or port keeps the probe independent.
pitfalls: A single-threaded cpp-httplib server serialises probes behind application requests - run it with a thread pool or on a dedicated health port, otherwise a slow request looks like an unhealthy instance.
Exceptions escaping a handler or an indicator must be converted (set_exception_handler/set_error_handler) or one broken check takes the whole endpoint down instead of reporting 503.
The registry is usually a shared object captured by the handler: without a mutex (or an immutable snapshot) every concurrent probe races with the workers updating the check state.
